The `epidist` package enables users to estimate delay distributions while accounting for common reporting biases.
This vignette first introduces the background [@park2024estimating] required to understand the models implemented in `epidist`.
It then goes on to explain each model in turn.

# Background {#maths}

Estimating a delay distribution may appear to be simple: one could imagine fitting a probability distribution to a set of observed delays.
However, observed delays are often biased during an ongoing outbreak.
We begin by presenting a formalism for characterizing delay distributions as well as two main biases (truncation and censoring) affecting them.
We then present statistical models for correcting for these biases.

Any epidemiological delay requires a primary (starting) and a secondary (ending) event.
For example, the incubation period measures the time between infection (primary event) and symptom onset (secondary event).
Here, we use $p$ to denote the time of the primary event, and $s$ to denote the time of the secondary event.

## Forwards and backwards distributions

We can measure any delay distribution in two different ways.
First, we can measure the forward distribution $f_p(\tau)$, starting from a cohort of individuals who experienced the primary event at the same time $p$ and looking at when they experienced their secondary event.
Second, we can measure the backward distribution $b_s(\tau)$, starting from a cohort of individuals who experienced the secondary event at the same time $s$ and looking at when they experienced their primary event.
While the length of each individual delay $\tau = p-s$ remains constant whether we look at it forward or backwards, the shape of the distribution is affected by the differences in perspectives due to the differences in cohort composition.

To illustrate their differences, let's assume that primary and secondary events occur at rates, or equivalently incidences, $\mathcal{P}(p)$ and $\mathcal{S}(s)$, respectively.
Then, the total density $\mathcal{T}(p, s)$ of individuals with a primary event at time $p$ and secondary event at time $s$ can be expressed equivalently in terms of both forward and backward distributions:
$$
\mathcal{T}(p, s) = \mathcal{P}(p) f_p(s - p)  = \mathcal{S}(s) b_s(s - p).  (\#eq:forwards-backwards)
$$
Rearranging Equation \@ref(eq:forwards-backwards) gives
$$
b_s(\tau) = \frac{\mathcal{P}(s - \tau) f_{s - \tau}(\tau)}{\mathcal{S}(s)}. (\#eq:forwards-backwards2)
$$
The denominator of Equation \@ref(eq:forwards-backwards2), which corresponds to the incidence of secondary events, may be expressed as the integral over all possible delays
$$
\mathcal{S}(s) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \mathcal{P}(s - \tau) f_{s - \tau}(\tau) \text{d} \tau,
$$
such that
$$
b_s(\tau) = \frac{\mathcal{P}(s - \tau) f_{s - \tau}(\tau)}{\int_{-\infty}^\infty \mathcal{P}(s - \tau) f_{s - \tau}(\tau) \text{d} \tau}.
$$
Here, we see that $b_s(\tau)$ depends not only on $f_{s - \tau}(\tau)$ but also on $\mathcal{P}(s - \tau)$, meaning that past changes in the incidence pattern will affect the shape of the distribution.
Particularly, when an epidemic is growing, we are more likely to observe shorter delays, causing an underestimation of the mean delay.
Therefore, we always want to characterize epidemiological delays from the forward perspective and estimate the forward distribution.
For this reason, our current methodology focuses on biases that affect the estimation of the forward distribution.

## Right truncation

One key bias that affects the forward distribution is right truncation.
Right truncation refers to the bias arising from the inability to observe future events and occurs when we observe data based on the secondary events.
For example, assume the data are right truncated and we don't observe secondary events past time $T$.
Then, we will only observe delays whose secondary events occurred before time $T$, causing us to underestimate the mean of the distribution as these delays will on average be shorter.

Bias from right truncation is greater when events are more likely to be more recent.
A common example of severely right truncated data is data collected during outbreaks when growth in incidence is exponential (so you are much more likely to have a recent event).
On the other hand, if data collection is continued until the end of an outbreak then many fewer events are likely to be more recent and so there will be little right truncation in general.

Mathematically right truncation can be described as follows.
Let $P$ and $S$ be random variables.
Let $F_p$ be the forward cumulative distribution.
Then, the probability of observing a delay of length $\tau$ given that the primary event occurred at time $p$ and a truncation at time $T$ can be written as:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(S = P + \tau \, | \, P = p, S < T) &= \frac{\mathbb{P}(S = P + \tau, P = p, S < T)}{\mathbb{P}(P = p, S < T)} \\
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}(S = P + \tau < T \, | \, P = p)\mathbb{P}(P = p)}{\mathbb{P}(S < T \, | \, P = p)\mathbb{P}(P = p)} \\
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}(S = P + \tau < T \, | \, P = p)}{\mathbb{P}(S < T \, | \, P = p)} \\
&= \frac{f_p(\tau)}{\int_0^{T - p} f_p(x) \text{d}x} = \frac{f_p(\tau)}{F_p(T - p)}, \quad p + \tau < T.
\end{aligned}
$$

Examining this equation illustrates that (right) truncation renormalises the density by the values which are possible.
For example, if the distribution $x \sim \text{Unif}(0, 1)$ were right truncated by $T = 0.5$ then $x \sim \text{Unif}(0, 0.5)$.

## Interval censoring

The exact timing of epidemiological events is often unknown.
Instead, we may only know that the event happened within a certain interval.
We refer to this as interval censoring.
A very common example of interval censoring in epidemiology is date censoring, where we only know, or are using, data to the day of an event rather than the precise time.
Other forms of interval censoring, like weekly or monthly interval censoring, are also common.
When both primary and secondary events are interval censored, this is referred to as double censoring.

Mathematically single interval censoring is defined as follows.
Assume the secondary event $S$ is censored and so we don't know when the event exactly happened.
Instead, we only know that the secondary event happened between $S_L$ and $S_R$.
Then,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(S_L < S < S_R \, | \, P = p) &= \int_{S_L}^{S_R} f_p(y-p) dy\\
&= F_p(S_R-p) - F_p(S_L-p)
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, double interval censoring is defined as follows.
Now, assume that both the primary $P$ and secondary $S$ events are truncated.
We only know that the primary event happened between $P_L$ and $P_R$ and the secondary event happened between $S_L$ and $S_R$.
We now write $g_P$ to denote the unconditional distribution of primary events.
Then,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(S_L < S < S_R \, | \, P_L < P < P_R) &= \mathbb{P}(P_L < P < P_R, S_L < S < S_R \, | \, P_L < P < P_R)\\
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}(P_L < P < P_R, S_L < S < S_R)}{\mathbb{P}(P_L < P < P_R)}\\
&= \frac{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} \int_{S_L}^{S_R} g_P(x) f_x(y-x) \,dy\, dx}{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} g_P(z)\, dz  }\\
&= \int_{P_L}^{P_R} \int_{S_L}^{S_R} g_P(x\,|\,P_L,P_R) f_x(y-x) \,dy\, dx
\end{aligned}
$$
where $g_P(x\,|\,P_L,P_R)$ represents the conditional distribution of primary event given lower $P_L$ and upper $P_R$ bounds.

# The naive model

The simplest approach to modelling epidemiological delay distributions is ignoring truncation and censoring biases and simply treating the delays as continuous fully observed data.
Then, the likelihood of observing a delay $\mathbf{Y}_i$ given parameter $\mathbf{\theta}$ is straightforward:
$$
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{Y}_i \, | \, \mathbf{\theta}) = f(y_i - x_i).
$$
where $y_i$ and $x_i$ are the observed primary and secondary event times.

As shown in [@park2024estimating]  when the data is double censored this modelling approach biases the mean by approximately a day as well as the standard deviation.
Where right truncation is also present biases can be more severe with plausible simulated scenarios leading to biased means that were >30% shorter than the true distributions.

# The latent model

This approach aims to account for the right truncation and double censoring using a generative modelling approach.
For each event, a latent variable is used to represent the exact time of the event.
This then allows the modelling of the continuous distribution, adjusted for the right truncation.
Whilst this is an approximation [@park2024estimating] showed good recovery of simulated distributions in a range of settings.
However, the use of two latent variables per observed delay means that this approach may scale poorly with larger datasets.
That being said this approach has been used successfully in multiple real-world outbreak settings ([@ward2022transmission]).
If using the latent model, please cite @park2024estimating in addition to `epidist`.

Mathematically this model is described as follows.
We look at the conditional probability that the secondary event $S$ falls between $S_L$ and $S_R$, given that the primary event $P$ falls between $P_L$ and $P_R$ and that the secondary event $S$ occurs before the truncation time $T$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{P}(S_L < S < S_R \, | \, P_L < P < P_R, S<T)\\
&= \mathbb{P}(P_L < P < P_R, S_L < S < S_R, S<T \, | \, P_L < P < P_R, S<T)\\
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}(P_L < P < P_R, S_L < S < S_R, S<T)}{\mathbb{P}(P_L < P < P_R, S<T)}\\
&= \frac{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} \int_{S_L}^{S_R} g_P(x) f_x(y-x) \,dy\, dx}{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} \int_{z}^T g_P(z) f_z(w-z) \, dz \,dw  }\\
&= \frac{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} \int_{S_L}^{S_R} g_P(x) f_x(y-x) \,dy\, dx}{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} g_P(z) F_z(T-z) \,dw  }\\
&= \frac{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} \int_{S_L}^{S_R} g_P(x|P_L, P_R) f_x(y-x) \,dy\, dx}{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} g_P(z|P_L, P_R) F_z(T-z) \,dw  }\\
\end{aligned}
$$
Using latent variables, we can now rewrite the observation likelihood as:
$$
\begin{aligned}
x_i &\sim g_P(x_i \, | \, p_{L, i}, p_{R, i}) \\
y_i &\sim \text{Unif}(s_{L, i}, s_{R, i}) \\
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{Y} \, | \, \mathbf{\theta}) &= \prod_i \left[ \frac{f_{x_i}(y_i - x_i)}{\int_{P_{L, i}}^{P_{R, i}} g_P(z \, | \, p_{L, i}, p_{R, i}) F_z(T - z) \text{d}z} \right].
\end{aligned}
$$
As before, $g_P(z \, | \, p_{L, i}, p_{R, i})$ represents the conditional distribution of the primary event given lower $P_L$ and upper $P_R$ bounds; this is equivalent to modelling the incidence in primary events.

## Bounding the latent primary event time {#latent-bound}

`epidist` samples both latent offsets on the unit scale.
Write $w_{P, i} = p_{R, i} - p_{L, i}$ and $w_{S, i} = s_{R, i} - s_{L, i}$ for the two censoring window widths.
Then
$$
\tilde{p}_i \sim \text{Unif}(0, 1), \qquad
\tilde{s}_i \sim \text{Unif}(0, 1), \qquad
s_i = w_{S, i}\, \tilde{s}_i,
$$
and the primary event offset is ordinarily
$$
p_i = w_{P, i}\, \tilde{p}_i .
$$

When the two censoring windows overlap the delay must still be non-negative.
The primary event therefore has to precede the sampled secondary event.
The offset is then bounded by the sampled secondary offset rather than by the window width.
$$
p_i = s_i\, \tilde{p}_i .
$$

That upper bound is itself a parameter.
The map $\tilde{p}_i \mapsto p_i$ therefore has Jacobian determinant
$$
\left| \frac{\partial p_i}{\partial \tilde{p}_i} \right| = s_i ,
$$
Stan does not add this term for a transformation written this way.
See the [Stan user's guide on changes of variables](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/reparameterization.html#changes-of-variables).
The log density of these observations needs it explicitly.
$$
\log \mathcal{L}_i \;\longmapsto\; \log \mathcal{L}_i + \log s_i .
$$
The non-overlapping case needs no such term because $w_{P, i}$ is data, so its Jacobian is a constant that cancels.
The primary event density is used unnormalised here.
A constant normalising it over $[0, s_i]$ would itself depend on $s_i$.

## A non-uniform primary event {#primary-tilt}

Incidence is not flat within a reporting window during rapid growth or decline.
Setting `primary = "expgrowth"` replaces the flat primary event with an exponentially tilted one at rate $r$.

The tilt is placed on the unit scale offset, with the rate scaled by that offset's bound $b_i$, which is $w_{P, i}$ ordinarily and $s_i$ where the windows overlap.
$$
\tilde{p}_i \sim \text{ExpGrowth}(0, 1, r_i b_i).
$$
Unlike the flat case, this density has to be normalised.
Its constant depends on $r_i$, which is estimated, so dropping it would let the likelihood grow without bound in $r_i$.

$r$ is a distributional parameter, so it takes a formula and a prior like any other.
This allows the rate to vary by covariate.
The delays carry little information about $r$.
It is normally taken from a separate estimate of epidemic growth and given an informative prior centred on that value, as in @brand2026scalable, rather than learned from the delays.
```r
epidist(data, formula = bf(mu ~ 1, pgrowth ~ 1 + region))
```

This follows the implementation in @brand2026scalable.

The latent model formulation follows @ward2022transmission.
The need for this adjustment was identified in @bdbvlinelist and derived in @brand2026scalable.

# The marginal model

The marginal model corrects for the same biases as the latent model but integrates out the exact event times numerically, or analytically where closed-form solutions exist, rather than sampling latent variables.
This approach uses the primary event censored distribution implemented in the [`primarycensored`](https://primarycensored.epinowcast.org/) package [@primarycensored].
If using the marginal model, please cite `primarycensored` in addition to `epidist`.

Under the assumption that the forward distribution does not change within the censoring interval (i.e. $f_x = f$ for $x \in [P_L, P_R]$), the double censoring probability from Section \@ref(interval-censoring) simplifies to
$$
\mathbb{P}(S_L < S < S_R \mid P_L < P < P_R) = \int_{P_L}^{P_R} g_P(x \mid P_L, P_R) \left[F(S_R - x) - F(S_L - x)\right] \text{d}x.
$$
For common delay and primary event distributions, such as gamma or lognormal delays with uniform primary events, `primarycensored` provides closed-form analytical solutions to this integral.
For other combinations, numerical integration is used.

Right truncation at time $T$ is handled by normalising the likelihood as in the latent model:
$$
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{Y} \mid \mathbf{\theta}) = \prod_i \frac{\mathbb{P}(S_{L,i} < S_i < S_{R,i} \mid P_{L,i} < P_i < P_{R,i})}{\int_{P_{L,i}}^{P_{R,i}} g_P(z \mid p_{L,i}, p_{R,i}) F(T - z) \, \text{d}z}.
$$

Removing the latent variables reduces the number of parameters that must be sampled, and where analytical solutions exist the likelihood can be evaluated without numerical integration.
In addition, identical observations can be aggregated and the likelihood computed once per unique combination of delay, censoring windows, and covariates.
Together these make the marginal model substantially more efficient than the latent model, particularly for larger datasets with daily-censored data where many observations share the same structure.

For the mathematical details of primary event censored distributions, including the survival function derivation and closed-form solutions for specific distributions, see `vignette("why-it-works", package = "primarycensored")` and `vignette("analytic-solutions", package = "primarycensored")`.

# The meta model

Published estimates are usually summary statistics rather than the individual delays the models above fit to, and the study's own estimation procedure is itself a source of bias [@charniga2024best; @park2024estimating].
The meta model fits one delay distribution to a mix of individual level data and published summaries.
Each summary is fitted to what the study's own estimation procedure would have converged to given the delay distribution, with sampling uncertainty from the study sample size.
That holds only where the metadata describing what the study did is correct.
The metadata is usually the analyst's judgement rather than something the study reported, so it should be stated explicitly and varied in a sensitivity analysis.
Study level heterogeneity, for example `mu ~ 1 + (1 | study)`, is specified through the `brms` formula, as for the other models above.
If using the meta model, please cite `primarycensored` in addition to `epidist`.
The meta model is experimental and its interface may still change.

## Sampling likelihoods {#sampling-likelihoods}

Let $f(\tau; \theta)$ and $F(\tau; \theta)$ be the forward density and distribution function of the delay of Section \@ref(maths).
Write $m_1$, $\sigma$, $\mu_3$ and $\mu_4$ for its mean, standard deviation, and third and fourth central moments, $\kappa = \mu_4 / \sigma^4$ for its kurtosis, $G$ for its distribution function and $Q_p$ for its quantile at probability $p$.
For a study that estimated the delay without bias these are the moments, distribution function and quantiles of $f(\cdot \, ; \theta)$ itself.
Section \@ref(the-biased-estimands) replaces them with those of the distribution the study's procedure targeted, and the likelihoods below are unchanged.
Each summary row reports a value $y$ and the sample size $n$ it was computed from.

### A reported mean

A reported mean is given a normal sampling distribution
$$
y \sim \text{Normal}\left(m_1, \; \text{se}_{m_1} \right), (\#eq:meta-mean-lik)
$$
where $\text{se}_{m_1}$ is the standard error reported by the study when one was given, and $\sigma / \sqrt{n}$ otherwise.

### A reported standard deviation

A reported standard deviation is given a normal sampling distribution with the kurtosis based asymptotic standard error of a sample standard deviation
$$
y \sim \text{Normal}\left(\sigma, \; \text{se}_\sigma \right), \quad
\text{se}_\sigma = \sigma \sqrt{\frac{\kappa - 1}{4 n}}. (\#eq:meta-sd-lik)
$$
This follows from the asymptotic variance of the sample variance, $(\mu_4 - \sigma^4)/n$, by the delta method [@cramer1946].
The normal theory expression $\sigma / \sqrt{2(n-1)}$ is the special case $\kappa = 3$, and is two to four times too narrow for the right skewed distributions delays usually follow.
Equation \@ref(eq:meta-sd-lik), and the pair likelihood of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-moment-pair) built on it, should not be trusted once the relative standard error $\sqrt{(\kappa - 1) / (4 n)}$ exceeds about a quarter.
For a lognormal with a log scale standard deviation of 0.5 that is $n$ below about 30.
`as_epidist_estimates_data()` warns when a reported mean and standard deviation imply this under a lognormal delay.

### A reported quantile

A reported quantile at probability $p$ is fitted on the cumulative probability scale, which avoids inverting $G$:
$$
p \sim \text{Normal}\left(G(y), \; \text{se}_p\right), (\#eq:meta-quantile-lik)
$$
where $\text{se}_p = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ is the binomial standard error of an empirical distribution function.
A quantile row supplied with a standard error $\text{se}_y$ on the delay scale is fitted on that scale instead,
$$
y \sim \text{Normal}\left(Q_p, \; \text{se}_y\right). (\#eq:meta-quantile-se)
$$

### Summaries from the same study

Summaries that one study computed from the same delays are correlated, so they are fitted jointly.
Two summaries are fitted together when they agree on every field other than the summary itself, that is on the study, its metadata, and any covariates supplied.
A summary supplied with its own standard error is fitted on its own.

A mean and a standard deviation from one study are given the asymptotic bivariate normal of the pair
$$
\begin{pmatrix} y_{m} \\ y_{\sigma} \end{pmatrix} \sim
\text{Normal}\left(
\begin{pmatrix} m_1 \\ \sigma \end{pmatrix}, \;
\frac{1}{n}\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma^2 & \mu_3 / (2 \sigma) \\
\mu_3 / (2 \sigma) & \sigma^2 (\kappa - 1) / 4
\end{pmatrix}
\right). (\#eq:meta-moment-pair)
$$
The off diagonal is $\text{Cov}(\bar{x}, s^2) = \mu_3 / n$ carried onto the standard deviation scale by the delta method [@cramer1946].
The implied correlation is $\gamma_1 / \sqrt{\kappa - 1}$, with $\gamma_1 = \mu_3 / \sigma^3$ the skewness, and $\kappa \ge \gamma_1^2 + 1$ holds for every distribution, so the covariance matrix is positive definite.
Moments computed numerically can sit a little outside that bound, so the correlation is held strictly inside $[-1, 1]$.

Several quantiles from one study at probabilities $p_1 < \dots < p_k$ with values $y_1 \le \dots \le y_k$ cut the delay axis into $k+1$ cells, and the number of delays in each is multinomial
$$
(c_1, \dots, c_{k+1}) \sim \text{Multinomial}\left(n, \; \left(G(y_1), \; G(y_2) - G(y_1), \; \dots, \; 1 - G(y_k)\right)\right), (\#eq:meta-quantile-set)
$$
with $c_j = \text{round}(n p_j) - \text{round}(n p_{j-1})$ and $c_{k+1} = n - \text{round}(n p_k)$.
A single quantile reduces Equation \@ref(eq:meta-quantile-set) to the binomial, of which Equation \@ref(eq:meta-quantile-lik) is the normal approximation, so quantile rows use Equation \@ref(eq:meta-quantile-set) unless the study supplied its own standard error.
Two quantiles reported at the same value are merged into one cell with their combined count.
A cell whose implied probability underflows to zero while the study saw delays in it has its probability floored at $10^{-300}$.

Summaries of different kinds from the same study, such as a mean and a median, are treated as independent, which understates their joint uncertainty.
The normal approximations degrade for small study sample sizes.

### A vector of summaries with a covariance

A study that fitted a distribution to its delays can publish draws of the fitted parameters, which `as_epidist_multivariate()` summarises by their mean and covariance and `as_epidist_estimates_data()` pushes through to the summaries the fitted distribution implies.
This is the reporting format we recommend, because it keeps the correlation between the reported quantities.
Writing $y$ for the reported vector and $\Sigma$ for the covariance over it,
$$
y \sim \text{Normal}\left(m(\theta), \; \Sigma\right), (\#eq:meta-mvn)
$$
where $m(\theta)$ holds the implied summary for each reported quantity, $m_1$ for a mean, $\sigma$ for a standard deviation and $Q_p$ for a quantile.
The covariance is supplied rather than derived from $n$, so a mixture of summary types need not be treated as independent.
Summaries of a $k$ parameter fit are functions of $k$ numbers, so at most $k$ of them have a non singular covariance, and asking for more is an error.

### Reported distribution parameters {#reported-distribution-parameters}

A study often publishes the parameters of a distribution it fitted rather than summaries of its delays.
`epidist_estimates_parameters()` converts them into the summaries the reported distribution implies, which are then fitted like any other reported summary.
Writing $\hat{F}$ for the reported distribution and $T$ for a summary, the reported value is $T(\hat{F})$ and the model compares it against $T$ of the distribution the study's procedure targeted.
Comparing summaries rather than parameters means the family a study fitted need not match the family being fitted to it.

Reported parameter standard errors are carried onto the summary scale by the delta method.
With $\hat{\theta}$ the reported parameters, $V$ the diagonal matrix of their squared standard errors, and $J$ the Jacobian of the map from parameters to summaries at $\hat{\theta}$, the covariance over the summaries is $J V J^\top$, and the summaries are fitted jointly with it through Equation \@ref(eq:meta-mvn).
Fitting $k$ summaries of a $k$ parameter fit this way gives the curvature $J^\top (J V J^\top)^{-1} J = V^{-1}$, so nothing is lost or invented by the conversion.
At most $k$ summaries can be reported with standard errors, and asking for more is an error.
A study that published a full parameter covariance can draw from it and pass the draws to `as_epidist_multivariate()`.
Where a study reported no parameter uncertainty, its summaries use the sample size likelihoods above, and any number of them may be reported.

This route assumes the summaries of the reported distribution are the summaries of what the study's procedure targeted, which holds only approximately where the study fitted a family of a different shape to its estimand, for example a continuous distribution to integer date differences.
Where the family cannot represent its own estimand, quantiles inside the body of the reported distribution are more reliable than a standard deviation, which depends on a tail the study never saw.

### Individual level records

Individual level rows use the marginal model likelihood of Section \@ref(the-marginal-model) unchanged, with $\theta$ shared with the summary rows.
Their primary event distribution is set with `primary`, so the tilted primary event of Section \@ref(primary-tilt) is available to them.
Summary rows take the growth rate given for each study as a known quantity rather than the estimated `pgrowth`, a limitation tracked in [epinowcast/epidist#678](https://github.com/epinowcast/epidist/issues/678).
The likelihood of the data is the product of the marginal model likelihood over the individual rows and of the sampling likelihoods above over the summary rows.

## What we need from each study

Forward modelling a published estimate needs to know how the study produced it.
For each summary we need:

* How it adjusted for interval censoring, one of no adjustment (it summarised integer date differences directly, the most common case), full adjustment (a double interval censored likelihood targeting the continuous distribution), the uniform single interval approximation (it adjusted the secondary interval assuming a uniform delay within it, and left the primary interval uncorrected), midpoint imputation (it assigned each delay to the centre of the interval it was observed in), or midpoint imputation with a uniform interval (it placed the primary event at the midpoint of its window and integrated the secondary interval).
* Whether the reported estimate was corrected for right truncation, and if it was not, the observation time, how collection stopped, and the growth rate of primary events over the study period.
  A cohort followed every primary event for the same observation time, which is the truncation point on the delay scale.
  A study that accrued primary events and stopped at a calendar date observed a given delay only for the primary events that occurred at least that long before the stop, and its observation time is the length of the collection window.
  Both corrections assume the study sampled a cohort of primary events, and so target the forward distribution of Section \@ref(forwards-and-backwards-distributions).
  A study that sampled on the secondary event, for example every death reported up to some date, reports a backward distribution, which is not represented here.
* The censoring windows, the width of the interval each event was observed in, for example 1 for daily reporting or 7 for weekly reporting.
* The sample size, or a reported standard error in its place, or a covariance matrix over the summaries it reported.
* The smallest delay it counted, where the study dropped delays below some point, so that its summaries describe a left truncated delay distribution.

Systematic reviews rarely record this metadata, so an assumption must be made and stated alongside any results.
The reporting checklist of @charniga2024best covers it.
Where the metadata is missing entirely, a covariate for the phase of the outbreak each estimate was made in makes the `brms` formula a meta-regression, estimating the residual bias rather than correcting it.

## The biased estimands {#the-biased-estimands}

For each setting of the metadata the study's procedure targeted a distribution other than $f(\cdot \, ; \theta)$.
The moments, distribution function $G$ and quantiles $Q_p$ of that distribution replace those of the delay in the likelihoods of Section \@ref(sampling-likelihoods).
The first four moments are needed, since those likelihoods use the mean, standard deviation, skewness and kurtosis.
Let $g_p$ be the distribution of a primary event within its censoring window of width $w_p$, uniform when incidence was constant over the study period and exponentially tilted towards more recent times when it was not.
Write
$$
F_{pc}(\tau; \theta) = \mathbb{P}(\tau^\star + U \le \tau), \quad \tau^\star \sim f(\cdot \, ; \theta), \; U \sim g_p,
$$
for the distribution function of the delay plus an independent primary event offset, which `primarycensored` provides.
Each estimand is right truncated at the study's observation time $D$, with $D = \infty$ for a study that adjusted for right truncation itself.

### Censoring adjustment

A study with no censoring adjustment summarised integer date differences directly, so its estimand is discrete.
Writing $q_j$ for the probability it puts on the $j$th secondary window,
$$
q_j = \frac{F_{pc}(j w_s; \theta) - F_{pc}((j-1) w_s; \theta)}{F_{pc}(w_s \lfloor D / w_s \rfloor; \theta)}, \quad j = 1, \dots, \lfloor D / w_s \rfloor, (\#eq:meta-grid)
$$
where $w_s$ is the secondary censoring window, bin $j$ carries the delay value $(j-1) w_s$, and the truncation point is discretised to the last full grid boundary.
This is the doubly interval censored, right truncated probability mass function of @primarycensored that the marginal model of Section \@ref(the-marginal-model) uses for individual observations.
Summing over the grid gives the moments, and its cumulative sum gives $G$.
For quantile rows $G$ is continuity corrected by interpolating the grid distribution function linearly through the mid points of its cells, because a reported quantile of day resolution data otherwise always lands on a jump of the step function.
The reported value is itself rounded to the grid, so a bias remains that does not shrink with the sample size.
It stays under 4% on the mean and 9% on the standard deviation once the reported quantiles sit twenty five or more cells above the smallest delay the study counted, and reaches tens of percent on both when they sit within ten, so a coarsely resolved delay is better fitted through its mean and standard deviation where a study reports them.

A single quantile of integer day delays is a discrete statistic.
"The median is 5 days" says that the empirical distribution function crossed one half between 4 and 5 days, that is $N_{\le y - w_s} < \lceil n p \rceil \le N_{\le y}$ with $N_{\le y}$ the number of delays at or below $y$.
It is fitted as the probability of that event,
$$
P(N_{\le y} \ge k) - P(N_{\le y - w_s} \ge k), \quad k = \lceil n p \rceil, \quad N_{\le y} \sim \text{Binomial}\left(n, G_0(y)\right), (\#eq:meta-quantile-crossing)
$$
where $G_0$ is the uncorrected distribution function of the grid.
The information this carries saturates as $n$ grows.
Several quantiles from such a study use Equation \@ref(eq:meta-quantile-set) on the continuity corrected $G$, which is calibrated at around thirty delays but claims a standard error five times too small at a thousand, so `as_epidist_estimates_data()` warns about such studies.

A study with full adjustment reported the moments of $f(\cdot \, ; \theta)$ itself, right truncated at $D$:
$$
\mathbb{E}[\tau^k \mid \tau \le D] = \frac{\int_0^D k t^{k-1} \left(F(D; \theta) - F(t; \theta)\right) \text{d}t}{F(D; \theta)}, \quad k = 1, \dots, 4, (\#eq:meta-trunc-moments)
$$
which reduces to the ordinary family moments when $D = \infty$.
Its distribution function is $F(y; \theta) / F(D; \theta)$.

A study using the uniform single interval approximation left the primary interval uncorrected, so it observed $\tau^\star + U$, and its moments are those of $F_{pc}$ right truncated at $D$:
$$
\mathbb{E}[(\tau^\star + U)^k \mid \tau^\star + U \le D] =
\frac{\int_0^D k t^{k-1} \left(F_{pc}(D; \theta) - F_{pc}(t; \theta)\right) \text{d}t}{F_{pc}(D; \theta)},
\quad k = 1, \dots, 4. (\#eq:meta-uniform-moments)
$$
Its distribution function is $F_{pc}(y; \theta) / F_{pc}(D; \theta)$.
Equations \@ref(eq:meta-trunc-moments) and \@ref(eq:meta-uniform-moments) are evaluated by Simpson's rule.
Where $D = \infty$ and the primary event distribution is uniform the convolution is exact:
$$
\mu_{pc} = \mu + \frac{w_p}{2}, \quad
\sigma_{pc}^2 = \sigma^2 + \frac{w_p^2}{12}, \quad
\mu_{4,pc} = \mu_4 + 6 \sigma^2 \frac{w_p^2}{12} + \frac{w_p^4}{80}, (\#eq:meta-uniform-exact)
$$
where $\mu$, $\sigma^2$ and $\mu_4$ are the mean, variance and fourth central moment of $f(\cdot \, ; \theta)$.

A study using midpoint imputation summarised the grid of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-grid) with bin $j$ carrying the delay value $(j - 1/2) w_s$ rather than $(j-1) w_s$.
Its mean is the grid mean plus $w_s / 2$, its central moments are unchanged, and its distribution function is the grid one evaluated at $y - w_s / 2$.
A single reported quantile uses Equation \@ref(eq:meta-quantile-crossing), as for no adjustment.

A study using midpoint imputation with a uniform interval placed the primary event at the midpoint of its window and integrated the secondary interval, so it observed $\tau^\star + U - w_p / 2$.
Its mean is that of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-uniform-moments) less $w_p / 2$, its central moments are unchanged, and its distribution function is that of the uniform single interval approximation evaluated at $y + w_p / 2$.
A study that midpointed the secondary interval and left the primary alone is midpoint imputation above.
Each code models the study as integrating the interval it did not midpoint rather than drawing one position within it, which would add $w^2 / 6$ to the variance.

### Right truncation

The truncation above conditions on the delay falling below a single cutoff, which is what a cohort followed for a common observation time gives.
This is truncation rather than right censoring, where a case is known to exist and contributes a survival term rather than being absent from the study.
Right censoring is not yet supported.

A study that accrued primary events over a window of length $A$ and stopped at its calendar end saw a delay of $d$ only for the primary events that occurred at least $d$ before the stop.
With primary events arriving at a rate proportional to $\exp(r t)$, the follow up available to such a delay is
$$
w(d) = \int_0^{A - d} \exp(r t) \, \text{d}t = \frac{\exp(r (A - d)) - 1}{r}, \quad 0 \le d \le A, (\#eq:meta-accrual)
$$
which tends to $A - d$ as $r$ tends to zero, and for a long window and a growing epidemic approaches an exponential tilt by $\exp(-r d)$.
This is the dynamical bias of @park2024estimating.
The estimand is $f(d; \theta) w(d)$ renormalised over $[0, A]$, with $A$ in place of the cohort cutoff $D$.
The weight multiplies the quadrature for Equations \@ref(eq:meta-trunc-moments) and \@ref(eq:meta-uniform-moments) at each node and renormalises.
For Equation \@ref(eq:meta-uniform-moments) it is evaluated at $d - w_p / 2$, to average the primary offset back out.
The correction is only as good as the growth rate supplied.

On the grid of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-grid) the follow up is a step function, $w(w_p \lfloor x / w_p \rfloor)$ for a delay of $x$ from the start of the primary window, whenever $A$ is a multiple of $w_p$.
Each cell of the grid is cut at the multiples of $w_p$ inside it, each piece is weighted by the follow up at the primary window it starts in, and the pieces are summed back into their cell before renormalising.
Weighting each cell at its lower edge instead is exact only when the windows are equal, and for a daily primary and weekly secondary window puts the implied mean 36% low at $r = 0.2$ where the piecewise weight is within 0.2%.

Two residuals remain.
The piecewise weight treats the last primary window as complete, so when $A$ is not a multiple of $w_p$ the primary events it cuts short are overweighted, by 5% on the mean for a weekly primary and daily secondary window with $A = 30$ at $r = 0.2$.
Use a collection window that is a multiple of the primary window where the study allows it.
Equation \@ref(eq:meta-uniform-moments) keeps the smooth weight, because the follow up available to a primary event is only known to within its window, and at $w_p = 7$ its implied mean is 2.6% high at $r = 0.2$.
Both residuals grow with the growth rate and as $w_p$ grows towards the length of the collection window.

### Left truncation

A study that only counted delays of at least $L$ reported summaries of a left truncated estimand, so every quantity above is conditioned on $\tau > L$ [@klein2003].
Each expression reduces to the form already given when $L = 0$.
On the grid of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-grid) the cells recording a delay below $L$ are dropped and the rest renormalised by the mass they hold, which is $F_{pc}(D) - F_{pc}(L)$ whenever $L$ falls on a grid boundary.
The truncated moments of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-trunc-moments) pick up a boundary term,
$$
\mathbb{E}[\tau^k \mid L < \tau \le D] =
\frac{L^k \left(F(D; \theta) - F(L; \theta)\right) +
\int_L^D k t^{k-1} \left(F(D; \theta) - F(t; \theta)\right) \text{d}t}
{F(D; \theta) - F(L; \theta)}, \quad k = 1, \dots, 4, (\#eq:meta-left-moments)
$$
and the same applies to Equation \@ref(eq:meta-uniform-moments) with $F_{pc}$ in place of $F$.
The distribution function becomes
$$
G(y) = \frac{F(y; \theta) - F(L; \theta)}{F(D; \theta) - F(L; \theta)}, \quad L < y \le D, (\#eq:meta-left-cdf)
$$
zero at or below $L$ and one above $D$.
The accrual weight of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-accrual) is unchanged.
Individual level rows pass $L$ to `primarycensored` as their left truncation point, as the marginal model does.

### Quantiles of the estimands

The quantile $Q_p$ of an estimand is read off by inverse linear interpolation between the two points of $G$ that bracket $p$.
On the grid of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-grid) that interpolant is the continuity corrected quantile, so it is exact.
For a continuous estimand the chord is refined, exactly through the family quantile function for a lognormal or weibull delay reported by a study that adjusted for censoring, and otherwise by two Newton steps using the closed form distribution function and density of the estimand.
An accrual estimand is defined by the interpolation between its nodes and keeps its chord.

### Summaries of a reported distribution

The summaries of a reported distribution $\hat{F}$ (Section \@ref(reported-distribution-parameters)) are taken over the range of delays the study could have seen, conditioning on $(L, D]$,
$$
\hat{F}_{L,D}(y) = \frac{\hat{F}(y) - \hat{F}(L)}{\hat{F}(D) - \hat{F}(L)}, \quad L < y \le D. (\#eq:meta-reported-cond)
$$
Summarising $\hat{F}$ over its whole support would charge a study that did not correct for right truncation with spread its data never had, which for a short observation time can reach tens of percent on a standard deviation.
A reported quantile at probability $p$ is the value $\hat{F}_{L,D}$ puts $p$ below.
